name: TRT / testosterone for jaw

lead: Some looksmaxxing users take testosterone replacement therapy (TRT), or discuss related androgens such as DHT, hoping for a more masculine jaw, midface and neck.

The chain is hormonal: testosterone acts on the androgen receptor and is converted in tissues to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), linked to facial and body hair growth, while testosterone is linked to musculoskeletal development, voice deepening and libido. Testosterone medication is approved for men with low natural testosterone, for masculinising therapy in transgender men and for some other uses. No study of testosterone for jaw or facial bone structure in appearance enhancement was found.

paras: In medical use it is prescribed after testing and monitored over time. Users in forums discuss it alongside training, body-fat reduction and facial hair as part of a broader masculinising routine. Muscle, skin and hair changes appear over months.

Reported effects include acne, oily skin, hair loss, breast enlargement in men, raised red blood cell count, worsened sleep apnoea, liver toxicity with some forms and suppression of sperm production. Testosterone is Schedule III in the US, Class C in the UK and prescription-only in the EU.

chain: Claimed facial bone and muscle change
angle.text: Users discuss testosterone therapy and related androgens as a route to a more masculine jaw, midface and neck. Testosterone therapy is established for low testosterone and masculinising treatment, but no study tests it for jaw structure.

lead: TRT or testosterone for jaw is a looksmaxxing belief that testosterone replacement therapy, or related androgens such as dihydrotestosterone (DHT), can make the face look more masculine: a wider, squarer jaw, a more prominent brow, facial hair, leaner skin-over-bone definition and more muscle in the neck and shoulders that frames the face. Forum members who discuss it link hormone levels to jaw and bone development, and some describe logging their aesthetic changes after starting therapy.[1][2]

Testosterone medication is an established treatment for men with low or absent natural production, for masculinising hormone therapy in transgender men and for certain breast cancers.[3] Clinical descriptions of masculinising therapy list facial changes as part of the effects of androgens: a more prominent brow, a broader and deeper jaw, a visible Adam's apple, plus facial hair growth, increased muscle and redistribution of fat away from the cheeks and lips.[4] Those effects are described mainly in people who start therapy after puberty with little prior androgen exposure.

Testosterone is converted in tissues to DHT by the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase, and DHT is linked to facial and body hair growth.[5] Medical sources also describe risks: acne, hair loss in people predisposed to it, breast enlargement in men, raised red blood cell count and suppressed sperm production.[3][6] No published study has tested testosterone therapy specifically for jaw or facial bone structure in men with normal development.

paras: The idea draws on how androgens shape the male face at puberty. Rising testosterone is associated with growth of the jaw and brow, thickening of facial hair and growth of muscle, and posts in looksmaxxing communities treat hormone levels as a lever for those traits.[1][7] Testosterone medication comes as injections, gels, patches, oral, buccal, nasal and implant forms.[3]
Related topics include DHT, which is made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase,[5] and drugs that block that enzyme, which members raise because of hair loss concerns when discussing androgens.[2]

Some of the most active forum discussions concern teenagers and bone growth. A looksmax.org thread from a user who says he is 16 asks whether higher androgen exposure would close growth plates faster, and replies show members trading anecdotes about bone development under hormone use.[1] Another thread asks whether testosterone would help normal development at 15 for a person with a chronic illness.[8] These posts are personal accounts rather than clinical records.

Reviews of testosterone replacement describe goals of improving libido, mood, muscle and bone mass and anaemia in men with deficiency.[9] European guidelines for functional hypogonadism stress diagnosing it from repeated low morning testosterone plus symptoms, and note lifestyle change and weight loss as first approaches in overweight men.[10]

In transgender men, androgen therapy is described as producing more prominent brows, a broader jaw, nose-tip enlargement, facial and body hair, deeper voice and greater muscle.[4] The reference notes that cheek and lip changes come from fat redistribution rather than bone.[4]

Reported effects of testosterone medication include acne, oily skin, scalp hair loss in the predisposed, breast enlargement in men, mood changes, raised haematocrit and worsened sleep apnoea.[3] Liver toxicity is associated with some oral forms.[3]

Exogenous androgens suppress gonadotropins and reduce testicular testosterone, which impairs sperm production; recovery after stopping is described as slow and variable.[6] A randomised trial in men with hypogonadism examined prostate safety events during testosterone therapy.[11]

Testosterone is a Schedule III controlled substance in the United States, Schedule IV in Canada, Class C in the UK and prescription-only in the EU, and it is banned in competitive sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency.[3] In February 2025 the FDA revised the boxed warning on testosterone products, removing cardiovascular language and adding a blood pressure warning.[3]

No studies found on testosterone for jaw or facial bone structure in the context of appearance. Related research covers hypogonadism: reviews of testosterone preparations and their pharmacokinetics,[9] guidelines on diagnosis and monitoring,[10] a randomised trial of sexual function and hypogonadal symptoms,[12] and a trial of prostate safety events.[11] A 2025 review covers testosterone replacement and spermatogenesis.[6]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, testosterone appears in threads about physique, bone development, hair loss and 'stacks', often alongside the abbreviations TRT and AI (aromatase inhibitor). Members debate hormone levels and facial outcomes in personal terms.[1][2][7]
